pages.x: About 3,000 years ago people of the Lapita culture, whose ancestors had come from Taiwan and the islands of Southeast Asia, sailed east into the open Pacific and settled Fiji, Tonga and Samoa. There, Polynesian culture was born.
They sailed in great double canoes, two hulls joined by a deck, with sails of woven pandanus leaves, carrying families, pigs, dogs, chickens and plants to start a new life.
pages.fx: They could beat back against the wind, so explorers could search for land and still find their way home.

pages.x: Navigators carried no instruments. They steered by the rising and setting stars, felt the ocean swells bounce off islands beyond the horizon, watched for land birds and clouds, and handed down their knowledge by memory and chant.

Between about 1000 and 1250 came a burst of long voyages. Polynesians reached Hawaii, Rapa Nui, which Europeans called Easter Island, and finally, around 1250 to 1300, Aotearoa, New Zealand: the last large land on Earth to be settled by people.

Polynesians were growing the sweet potato, a plant from South America, long before Europeans came. Their sailors probably reached South America and brought it back, and DNA studies suggest that Polynesians and Native Americans met around 1200.

On Rapa Nui, some 2,000 km from any other inhabited island, people carved nearly 1,000 giant stone figures of their ancestors, the moai. Islanders say the statues walked, and experiments show they could be rocked upright along the ground with ropes.

European sailors later doubted that Polynesians could have found their islands on purpose. In 1976 the double canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti, over 4,000 km, guided only by the stars and the sea by the navigator Mau Piailug. It proved they could.

Polynesians settled a triangle of ocean bigger than Russia, centuries before Europeans dared to cross the open sea. Their way of finding islands is being taught again, a proud part of the identity of Hawaiians, Māori and other Pacific peoples.
pts: Settled nearly every island of the Pacific
Reached New Zealand last, around 1250 to 1300
